weeks.worstPlay: Abe not using the spy on Ali.
weeks.summary:
The lights hum.

Too loud. Too constant.

Hussein rocks back and forth in a narrow room, eyes locked on a Catan board bolted to the table.

It never resets.

It never forgives.

“They gave it to me…” he whispers.

His fingers trace invisible placements.

“Hassan… Dania… what were they doing?”

A twitch. Then a laugh.

“Suboptimal. Completely suboptimal.”

His voice sharpens.

“They handed me the game.”

His breathing quickens.

“Sheep port. Perfect numbers. Everything flowing…”

His head tilts.

“I had the best setup.”

Silence.

Then—

The dice.

Echoing.

Eights.

Again.

Again.

Again.

“I was printing resources,” he mutters faster now. “I rushed aqueduct—I was ahead—I was always ahead—”

His voice snaps.

“And then I didn’t activate knight.”

Dead silence.

His eyes widen.

“No knight… no paper…”

His hand slams the table.

“My city.”

Gone.

A long pause.

Then a whisper:

“They kept stealing from me.”

His head jerks side to side.

“Even after I lost it… even after I wasn’t ahead…”

His voice cracks—

“Because Ali told them I was.”

A shaky breath.

A laugh that doesn’t land.

“He can’t keep getting away with this…”

His eyes dart.

“He can’t keep winning.”

The board shifts.

Faster now.

“I fixed it,” Hussein blurts, pacing. “I had it under control—I had a plan—”

Two cards.

Clutched tight.

“Inventor.”

His voice rises.

“I hit him. I HIT ALI.”

A jab at the board.

“I took his 9. I broke his 5. I turned them into nothing—4 and 3—”

A pause.

Hope.

“I solved it.”

The dice roll.

Loud.

Closer.

“…the 3.”

His breathing stutters.

“No.”

Again.

“The 3.”

Again.

“The 3.”

He grabs his head.

“IT KEPT ROLLING.”

His voice cracks into panic.

“And he—he used the wheat port—”

A step back.

“He took the paper metropolis.”

A whisper now:

“Mine…”

His back hits the wall.

“He can’t keep getting away with this…”

Louder now—

“He can’t keep winning!”

The room feels tighter.

Closing in.

“I lost another city.”

His voice is thinner now, stretched.

“I thought I’d be safe. I thought this time—this time—”

He shakes his head violently.

“No. No. No.”

Voices echo.

Fragments.

“Abe…”

Hussein freezes.

“Abe had the spy.”

His eyes go wide.

“Four development cards. Four.”

His hands tremble.

“It was obvious…”

A sudden explosion:

“IT WAS OBVIOUS!”

He slams the wall.

“He uses it on DANIA?!”

His voice spirals upward.

“Not Ali. Not the four cards. Not the threat—”

A laugh, high and unstable:

“And now he has TWO MERCHANTS.”

He starts pacing in tight circles.

“Worst play of the day worst play of the day worst play of the day—”

He stops abruptly.

Still.

“I rebuilt.”

A fragile whisper.

“I came back.”

A flicker of hope.

“I got my city again…”

A smile tries to form.

It fails.

“And then Dania…”

His face empties.

“She had the point.”

A long pause.

“She could have taken it.”

His breathing becomes uneven.

“And I lost my city again.”

Silence crashes down.

Then—

A whisper, trembling:

“He can’t keep getting away with this…”

His head lifts suddenly.

“Rasha.”

Hope.

Desperate.

“She just had to take Abe’s deal.”

A beat.

A break.

“But she didn’t.”

His voice fractures—

“Why didn’t she take my deal…?”

His hands tremble violently now.

“It was my deal…”

Louder—

“IT WAS A FAIR DEAL!”

His voice cracks into something raw:

“She’s my wife…”

A long, hollow pause.

The room spins faster.

“Okay okay okay still winnable still winnable—”

His hands shake uncontrollably.

“Ali’s at twelve…”

A pause.

“One away.”

His voice collapses:

“ONE AWAY FROM THIRTEEN.”

He looks around the empty room, eyes pleading.

“I just needed paper.”

Nothing answers.

“I asked. I begged. Anyone.”

His voice rises into desperation:

“ANYONE.”

A whisper:

“Abe had it.”

A long, hollow silence.

“He said… he didn’t hear me.”

Something in Hussein breaks.

Completely.

“No one stopped him,” he says faintly.

“No one.”

His breathing slows.

Too slow.

A final realization settling in like weight.

Not luck.

Not mistakes.

Not even chaos.

Just—

Him.

Ali.

Always one step ahead.

Hussein’s head tilts back.

His voice erupts—raw, cracked, unrecognizable:

“HE CAN’T KEEP GETTING AWAY WITH THIS!”

A beat.

Then louder—

“HE CAN’T KEEP WINNING!”

And finally, everything shatters into one last scream:

“I DESERVED TO WIN, ALI!”

The lights buzz.

The board stays.

Unchanged.

And somewhere—

Outside this room…

Ali reaches thirteen.

And wins.

weeks.recapTitle: Catan Court: The People vs. Last Week’s Decisions
weeks.bestPlay: Hussein's placement on the wheat port and then getting all of the best wheat spots to have an ultimate setup.
weeks.worstPlay: Rasha for using her Master Merchant after getting more points than Hussein.
weeks.summary:
All rise.

The Court of Catan is now in session.
The Honorable Judge Ali Beidoun presiding.

You may be seated.

Court has been called today to address a series of... questionable decisions made during last week’s game. Rather than reviewing yet another victory (mine), we will instead be examining the defendants’ conduct and issuing rulings accordingly.

Hussein will be serving as court clerk and occasional advisor-though based on recent events, he may also be subject to cross-examination.

Let’s proceed.

Count I: Lena - Failure to Appear / Jury Duty Evasion

Lena, please... actually, never mind. The court notes your absence.

You are charged with failure to appear after being properly summoned, as well as evasion of jury duty.

Let the record reflect: you were expected in court. You did not attend.

Now, the court understands that work obligations may arise. However, upon review, there was no evidence of an imminent deadline, emergency filing, or last-minute injunction that would justify absence.

“General work responsibilities” are no longer a valid excuse for missing game night.

This court runs on consistency, commitment, and occasionally poor decision-making-but attendance is non-negotiable.

Verdict: Guilty (in absentia).
Sentence: Mandatory appearance at the next session.

Count II: Hassan - Reckless Use of a Deserter

Hassan, please approach.

You are charged with reckless Deserter usage.

You played the card. Twice.

And yet-you had nowhere to place the knight.

We do not summon knights without jurisdiction.

Verdict: Guilty.

Count III: Abe - Failure to Prevent an Imminent Win

Abe, step forward.

Rasha was about to win. You had the Merchant.

And you chose... inaction.

There is no appeal once the game is over.

Verdict: Guilty.

Count IV: Abe - Misguided Prosecution

You focused your efforts on targeting me.

The objective is not to take me down. The objective is to win.

Verdict: Guilty.

Count V: Dania - Failure to Utilize Available Remedies

You had the Merchant. Rasha was at 12 points.

And you... decided that was enough for the turn.

Failure to act is worse than acting incorrectly.

Verdict: Guilty.

Count VI: Hussein - Hoarding Without Execution

You had thirty cards and a wheat port.

And did nothing.

Holding assets without execution is not strategy.

Verdict: Guilty.

Count VII: Dania - Failure to Anticipate a Known Outcome

You had the chance to block my road.

You didn’t.

I connected, took Longest Road, and won.

Verdict: Guilty.

Count VIII: Rasha - Procedural Misconduct Leading to Loss

You had the win.

You used your Master Merchant in the wrong order.

What you should have done:
Use it first
Take resources
Build
Win

What you did:
Wrong order
Three cards
No win

Order matters.

Verdict: Guilty.

Court is adjourned.

The judge remains undefeated.

weeks.worstPlay: Lena for not using her 30 cards to break Rasha's road and stop her from winning.
weeks.summary:
The tavern was loud that night-tankards clashing, firelight dancing across stone walls, and the low murmur of strategy whispered like conspiracies. The board was set. Not a battlefield of swords and steel, but of hexes and roads, cities and cunning. And seated at its center, calm as a queen before war, was Rasha Kaleesi.

They underestimated her.

At first, it seemed like any other game. Settlements rose modestly, roads stretched cautiously across the land, and the other players-lords of wheat and brick, barons of ore-made their moves with quiet confidence. They traded politely. They built predictably.

Rasha did neither.

She watched.

Like a dragon circling high above, she studied every move, every hesitation, every alliance forming in hushed tones. Then, without warning, she struck.

Her expansion was swift and ruthless. Where others hesitated, she claimed. Where resources were scarce, she controlled the flow. Ore and wheat bent to her will, and soon her cities rose-tall, unshakable, inevitable. The board began to change shape, no longer a fair kingdom but a realm under quiet conquest.

And then came the knights.

Not mere tokens, but her army. While others hoarded cards or chased fleeting victories, Rasha built strength-turn after turn, knight after knight. Her forces grew, vigilant and ready. And when the barbarians came, it was she who stood prepared.

The others faltered.

Their defenses were weak, their planning shortsighted. When the barbarians struck, it was not just a loss-it was humiliation. Cities fell. Progress crumbled. And through it all, Rasha remained untouched, her knights defending the realm with precision.

Whispers spread around the table. Alliances formed against her. Trades were denied. Desperation crept in.

It didn't matter.

Rasha adapted. Where she was blocked, she pivoted. Where she was challenged, she dominated. Progress cards became weapons in her hands-monopolies that drained her enemies, inventions that accelerated her rise, and cunning plays that left others stunned in silence.

One by one, the players fell behind.

A lord of sheep was reduced to begging for brick. A master of roads found his expansion strangled. Even the most confident among them began to unravel, their strategies collapsing under the weight of her control.

By the time they realized the truth, it was already over.

Rasha Kaleesi did not just play the game.

She ruled it.

Her final city rose like a crown upon the board, and with it came victory-undeniable, absolute. The tavern fell quiet for a moment, the weight of what had just happened settling in.

Then someone laughed nervously.

"Rematch?"

Rasha only smiled.

Because in that moment, they all understood: this was never just a game of Catan.

It was conquest.

weeks.recapTitle: Misunderstood: The Tom Ali Riddle Story
weeks.bestPlay: Ali getting the coin metropolis even though he wasnt on ore
weeks.worstPlay: Dania for protecting Catan instead of letting Hassan lose his city
weeks.summary:
They will tell you I was born to dominate the board.

They will say I arrived with ambition in my eyes, that I chose power-that I craved it.

But they never tell you how it began.

I remember the orphanage.

Cold. Bare. Predictable in its cruelty. You learned quickly there that if you did not take your place, someone else would take it from you. That resources were never given-only denied.

So when I sat at the table that night, I did what I had learned long ago.

I, Tom Ali Riddle, chose well.

Two strong settlements. A future unfolding. A quiet, careful path toward something more. For a fleeting moment, I believed that this time, things might be different.

But as I once said, there is no good and evil, there is only power... and those too weak to seek it.

And they had already decided I was not allowed to seek it.

Ginny Dania Weasley was the first.

She placed her city beside mine. Not for growth. Not for strategy.

For containment.

A deliberate cut. My path to the sheep port-gone.

Then came Snape Hussein.

He didn't just harm me. He harmed himself to do it. The kind of loyalty that says: I will suffer, so long as you suffer more.

And still, I endured.

But it was Harry Hassan Potter and Hermione Linda Granger who sealed the narrative.

Two roads. Immediate. Calculated.

Not to build.

To trap.

I could see it then. The board shrinking around me, piece by piece, like the walls of that orphanage closing in once more. Every path denied. Every option suffocated.

There was one move left.

All I needed was wood.

One piece.

A single act of mercy from a table that had already judged me.

"Trade?" I asked.

Silence.

Or worse-smiles.

They will say I was dangerous. That they had no choice.

But what kind of "good" refuses even the smallest chance for someone to survive?

It is our choices that show what we truly are... and theirs were made long before mine.

The robber came.

Snape Hussein again.

He took what little I had left, as if to remind me: you are not meant to rise.

Harry Hassan Potter and Hermione Linda Granger built again.

The final door closed.

"I have no chance of winning," I said.

And I meant it.

But I did not become who I am because I always had power.

I became who I am because I learned how to live without it.

Greatness inspires envy, envy engenders spite, spite spawns lies.

And oh, how they lied about me.

Rita Lena Skeeter made sure of that.

Ever watchful, ever whispering.

"He's not to be trusted."

Again.

And again.

And again.

But then her quill turned.

Not toward me.

Toward them.

A scathing article.

Sharp. Calculated. Precise.

She wrote of cracks forming between Harry Hassan Potter and Hermione Linda Granger-questioning their alliance, their shared road, their intentions. What once was unity now looked like ambition. What once was partnership now felt like strategy.

She successfully broke their shared road, and their once near certain victory was halted.

And the moment their shared road was broken, the balance shifted.

While they turned, even slightly, against one another-

another rose.

Snape Hussein.

The Half-Road Prince.

What Rita Lena Skeeter disrupted, he seized.

With their path fractured, the board opened-not for them, but for him.

While eyes were elsewhere, he advanced quietly, methodically. His network growing. His position strengthening. Not loud. Not flashy.

Inevitable.

He stepped into the space they left behind and stood at the edge of victory.

Closer than anyone realized.

And still I remained.

Forgotten.

Dismissed.

Finished.

So I let them believe it.

"I'm just here to roll dice," I said.

And they laughed.

But I remembered the orphanage.

I remembered what it felt like to have nothing.

And I, Tom Ali Riddle, began again.

Brick by brick.

Road by road.

Quietly.

Carefully.

While knights closed in.

While spells of defense were cast.

While luck-their luck-fell endlessly into place.

I built.

And then, from the shadows, came something I had nearly forgotten existed.

Kindness.

Peter Abe Pettigrew.

They will mock him.

But in that moment, he was the only one who saw me not as a threat, but as something human.

He gave me wood.

Just one.

And it was everything.

And that is when Snape Hussein broke.

A flash of anger. Sharp. Uncharacteristic.

Annoyed-not at the board, not at the game-

but at him.

At Peter Abe Pettigrew.

For choosing me.

For helping me rise.

His voice cut through the table, low and bitter.

And then, quieter-

"Her eyes..."

A pause.

"I did it... for Lily Rasha Potter's eyes."

And for a second, even I understood him.

But the board does not wait for grief.

And neither did I.

Help will always be given at Hogwarts to those who ask for it.

I asked.

And for once, someone answered.

The board opened.

The path returned.

For the first time since the beginning, I felt it.

Hope.

Rita Lena Skeeter's voice grew sharper.

"I told you... he’s not to be trusted."

But what she meant was: he is rising.

I was nearly there.

After everything, I stood at the edge of something impossible.

A victory not given.

A victory earned.

And then-

him.

Harry Hassan Potter.

There has always been something strange between us.

A connection neither of us understood.

As if part of me lived in him.

And in the end, it was him.

He took it.

The win.

The moment.

The story.

Just like that.

And they will tell you that good prevailed.

That the heroes triumphed.

That I was defeated once more.

But that is not the truth.

The truth is this:

I was never given a fair beginning.

I was denied, cornered, and cast aside.

I was called dangerous long before I had the power to be.

And when I finally rose-

they took it from me.

So if you ask me what I became that night...

I will not say villain.

I will not say monster.

Only this:

I am what they made me.

I am Voldemort.

weeks.recapTitle: The Pride Lands of Catan: Simba Hussein's Return
weeks.bestPlay: Hussein for stealing two metropolis for the win.
weeks.worstPlay: Abe for wasting two deserter cards by completely outsmarting himself and going for the aqueduct instead of going for the win.
weeks.summary:
The Pride Lands of Catan had fallen quiet.

Ali Mufusa, the great ruler of the board, had vanished beyond the horizon... and with him, balance left the land.

In his absence, darkness crept in.

From the shadows rose Abe Scar, who seized control of the Pride Lands with ruthless precision. Cities rose under his command. Knights marched at his bidding.

With two metropolises, powerful knights, and Dania the Hyena at his side, he believed himself untouchable.

No one dared challenge him.

Not Hassan Zazu, who found himself trapped early-boxed in, wings clipped, watching helplessly from his proverbial cage.

Not even Rasha Nala, who stood on the edge of defeat, her voice filled with frustration.

"It is over," she declared. "Scar has already won."

Her record weighed on her-0-7.
Her betrothed, Hussein Simba, was worse-0-9, missing, absent, gone from the Pride Lands.

Hope was fading.

Meanwhile, Linda Rafiki, self-proclaimed African queen, spoke in cryptic tongues-her words flowing like riddles no one could decipher.

"I am the queen of the Congo!" she proclaimed, as chaos unfolded.

Scar grew arrogant.

"I am the ruler of Catan," he boasted. "No one can stop me."

And for a time... he was right.

Desperate, Nala made a bold move.

With a whisper carried across the winds of the board, she cast an evil eye-declaring Scar the victor before he had truly won. An evil eye stretched from the Pride Lands to the outlands.

But even magic could not restore what was missing.

Simba.

Far from the board, hidden from destiny, Hussein Simba had abandoned his path.

"I am not Ali," he said. "I cannot rule like him. I cannot win."

Nala found him, her voice breaking.

"We cannot live like this," she pleaded. "The Pride Lands are lost."

But Simba turned away.

"I am not who you think I am."

And so Nala left... her hope nearly gone.

Then came Rafiki.

"Ali is here," she said.

Simba scoffed. "That makes no sense."

"I will show you."

The Catan board itself seemed to awaken.

As Scar took an eternity-fifteen long minutes-to incorrectly use two deserter cards... and a vision appeared.

From the sky... from the board... from within-

Ali Mufusa.

"Simba," he said.

"I'm not like you," Simba replied. "I can't rule the Pride Lands of Catan for four weeks. I don't have it in me."

Ali's voice echoed like thunder across the hexes:

"Remember who you are."
"Take your place... in the Circle of Catan."

Something changed.

Simba rose.

He returned to the Pride Lands.

And the comeback began.

First-he struck Dania the Hyena, seizing her metropolis.

Then, from the sidelines, Hassan Zazu made his move-blocking Scar, denying him the knight victory points he needed. A small act... but a crucial one.

Next, Rasha Nala, no longer defeated, rose with him-striking Scar and taking one of his metropolises.

The Pride Lands stirred.

Scar faltered.

Then came the final moment.

Simba faced Scar.

With one decisive move-swift, precise, undeniable-

He stole Scar's second metropolis.

The board fell silent.

The tyrant had fallen.

And so, at last-

Hussein Simba ascended.

Standing atop Pride Rock, in the center of the board, he claimed his place in the Circle of Catan.

Beside him stood Rasha Nala.

Above him, unseen but ever present, Ali Mufusa watched.

The first victory.

The rightful king had returned.

weeks.recapTitle: Rasha Umbridge: I will have order!
weeks.bestPlay: Hussein used his entire hand to produce 4 coin, securing the Coin Metropolis and giving him his only shot at victory.
weeks.worstPlay: Rasha Umbridge forced a departed Dania to produce on her numbers so she could try to steal her wood.
weeks.summary:
The game began, as most do, in deceptive calm.

But not all was ordinary.

Dania the Free Elf shocked the table early with one of the plays of the year — committing fully to the sheep port. It was bold. It was risky. And it paid off immediately, giving her a commanding early advantage.

Meanwhile, Hassan Weasley and Ali Potter stumbled out of the gates, their resources dry and their prospects uncertain. Across the board, Linda Lovegood wandered aimlessly, seemingly detached from reality — or perhaps simply ahead of it.

But two players had only one goal: survival.

Rasha Umbridge and Hussein Longbottom, both still chasing their first win of the year, came out with a level of desperation that could be felt across the island.

And Rasha?

She came to rule.

**The Rise of Umbridge**

“I will have order!”

And she did.

With ruthless efficiency, Rasha built her empire — roads stretching across the island, resources flowing, control tightening. When she seized Longest Road from Dania the Free Elf, it was over.

Or so it seemed.

She reached 12 points.

One card away.

Victory was inevitable.

**The Rebellion Forms**

But Catan does not bow to tyrants.

The Dumbledore’s Army assembled.

Ali Potter, quietly biding his time, made his move. With a calculated play, he used the Alchemist card, bending fate itself. He handed Dania the Free Elf a sock — and with it, freedom.

Two roads were built.

Longest Road was taken back.

Hope returned.

**Umbridge Strikes Back**

“Punishments cannot be adjusted…”

As Dania exited — freed, but gone — Rasha seized her moment. With a knight, she dismantled Dania’s roads and reclaimed Longest Road once more.

“I will have order!”

And again, she did.

The rebellion faltered. The table held its breath. Catan stood on the brink of total control.

**The Unexpected Hero**

Out of nowhere… Linda Lovegood.

In a move no one saw coming, she calmly built two roads and stole Longest Road from Umbridge.

Silence.

Then chaos.

Rasha began searching the table, her patience gone.

“You are not qualified to decide…”

Her control was slipping.

**The Fall Begins**

That single moment changed everything.

With Umbridge destabilized, Ali Potter and Hussein Longbottom surged forward, overtaking her lead.

And Rasha?

She was fuming.

Her face — as pink as her outfit — betrayed the truth:

“You deserve to be punished.”

**One Last Twist**

Ali Potter stood on the edge of victory.

But in true Lovegood fashion, Linda intervened again — stopping his Largest Army, and unintentionally reopening the door for Umbridge.

Rasha seized the opportunity.

She reclaimed Longest Road.

Now, she needed just one brick to win.

One.

**The Final Betrayal**

But Catan is cruel.

Linda needed just one road to take it back.

Ali traded her exactly what she needed.

And just like that—

Longest Road was stolen again.

Rasha exploded.

“I will have order!”

But there was no order left.

Her victory — once certain for over an hour — was gone.

“A lifelong ban ought to do the trick.”

**The Ending No One Expected**

In the chaos, Hassan Weasley, briefly unsure whether he was Ginny Weasley, rediscovered himself and mounted a late comeback.

But it was too late.

Because in the end…

The hero always wins.

Ali Potter claimed victory.

And the reign of Rasha Umbridge came to a dramatic, unforgettable end.

Note to Dania the Free Elf: Abe at Gringotts Wizarding Bank is the official record keeper for the game, and all complaints may be directed to him.

weeks.bestPlay: Hussein looked in pole position for the wool metropolis and the win and then Dania out of no where used her cards to get the wool metropolis.
weeks.worstPlay: Hussein, salty as can be about forgeting the rules, was only in this position because he let Ali take the paper metropolis over Hassan.
weeks.summary:
Today at Catan Downs, the 3rd Annual Coolidge Derby delivered one of the tightest finishes we’ve ever seen—a true photo finish for the ages.

The pre-Derby ceremonies started out with some real tension as Abe openly questioned if Dania was even going to show up. Officials had to pull Hassan off Abe as he was yelling keep my wife's name out your fucking mouth!

Out of the gates, Hussein surged ahead and quickly took control of the race, looking like the clear favorite as the pack rounded toward the final stretch. For most of the run, it seemed like his race to lose. But as they hit the homestretch, the field tightened dramatically. Abe, Hassan, and Ali all made their push, closing the gap until four contenders were neck and neck, each just one turn away from victory. Abe needed a coin. Ali needed two roads and Hassan just needed to get to his turn. Hussein was so busy defending his lead he forgot he needed to finish the race.

In the final moments, it all came down to the roll. Ali got exactly what he needed—and crucially, he was just ahead of Hassan in the order—giving him the chance to play his cards and surge past the pack to steal the win right at the line. A stunning comeback and a third straight Coolidge Derby title.

Doctor Lena deserves credit for an admirable ride, doing everything she could to prevent the three-peat. She pressed Ali hard against the rails and denied him clean opportunities to make his move, executing her strategy to near perfection. In the end, though, it wasn’t quite enough to hold him off.

Dania made what was arguably the best move of the day, but she made some stupid ass moves as Hassan said repeatedly. First, she used trade monopoly and got zero cards and then she built aimlessly into the desert for a reason no one can explain. She seemed content to enjoy the race, roll the dice, and be part of the action.

After the finish, tensions flared. Hussein, stunned at the result, cried foul and even attempted to have Ali disqualified. The matter was brought before Judge Rasha, who surprised everyone. Despite previously expressing hope that Hussein would win, she ruled firmly against him, noting that Hussein hardly needed the rules explained—especially given how often he corrects Abe on them weekly.

In the post-race coverage, announcer Rola praised Ali’s incredible finish and rightful victory, while also calling out Hussein for not knowing the rules and shifting the blame. Fair is fair.

Meanwhile, announcer Linda didn’t hold back, loudly criticizing the rest of the field for allowing Ali to claim a third straight Derby. She’s already declared her intention to join the race next week—though if her commentary is any indication, she may find herself finishing near the back of the pack.

A legendary race, a dramatic finish, and a three-peat for Ali—Catan Downs won’t soon forget this one.

weeks.recapTitle: Some Guys Have All the Luck
weeks.bestPlay: Dania building on Hussein's port and knocking him out of the game early.
weeks.summary: We're going to keep this short and sweet. Hassan got attacked. Abe got longest road and then got attacked. Ali didn't get attacked-and won.

weeks.recapTitle: Abe and the Terrible, Horrible, No Good, Very Bad Day
weeks.bestPlay: Ali for the resource monopoly heard about the world.
weeks.worstPlay: Rasha for not using the inventor on Ali’s spot even though he was about to win.
weeks.summary:
Sometimes prayers go unanswered and people lose faith. This week, the last ray of hope was taken from the settlers as Ali ran roughshod over the rest with a dominating—and for some, humiliating—loss. Sheik Hussein was heard wondering whether he’d be better off worshiping a different deity next week after his last-place finish this week.

There’s not much to be said about this bloodbath. The turning point in the game came when Abe spent about 15 minutes scratching his head, trying to make 3 for 1 deals, making us all wonder what he was up to. All of that ended up with him turning in his hand for three ore. The settlers waited for his next move and in amazement, he said, “It’s time for free play,” with the three ore in his hand. The very next turn, Ali used Resource Monopoly on ore and stole five ore from the settlers, including two Abe had worked tirelessly for. In a savage play, Ali also took two ore from Hassan just after he had finally gathered enough for a city. Abe simmered and stewed for the rest of the game, trying to seek revenge, but at that point it was a fait accompli.

Rasha had her third moral victory in a row, beating High Priest Hussein from the Satanic Society in Garden City.

Well, at least soon-to-be Dr. Lena showed up and played a respectable game.

Hassan played this game just to make sure everyone knew Dania was still the reigning champion. Since she didn’t play this week, he spared himself from another night sleeping on the ground.

weeks.bestPlay: Ali for stealing Hassan's coin metropolis in one turn and costing Hassan the game.
weeks.worstPlay: Hassan and Rasha for giving Dania the wool metropolis without a fight.
weeks.summary:
Catan is a battle. And sometimes that battle becomes a war.

This week's matchup was all-out war because Hussein, with the bravado of Napoleon Dynamite and the bite of a chihuahua, declared his prolonged losing streak would end tonight.

Like World War II, there were heroes. This week's hero, to the surprise of many, was Dania.

Dania is an inspiration to every young mother. Just six weeks postpartum, she returned from maternity leave with her baby on her lap and a bottle in her hand. She shocked us all by getting a win before the hosts.

In World War II, we had Rosie the Riveter. In the war declared by Hussein, we have Dania the Humble. She was the most unassuming champion, and she spent the evening thanking each of us individually for her victory in a way that felt anything but humble.

In war, there are winners and losers, and there were two big losers this evening. First was Ali, whose game sputtered from the start. He had an ideal opening strategy, which Hussein promptly jinxed by asking everyone to start over the moment Ali placed his starting spots. However, the biggest loser of the night was Abe. Abe went from worst to first and spent the rest of the evening exasperated because nothing he tried worked. By the end, both of them were basically just rolling dice and waiting for suhoor.

Morale victories do not mean much in wars, but for Rasha, that was as good as it gets right now. It was another close call, and she also tied for worst play of the week with Hassan.

In wars, you have to execute. Hassan had a great battle plan, had the spots, had the rolls, and still could not finish. The best play of the day came when Ali stole Hassan's metropolis with nine coins in a single turn, right before Hassan was about to win the game. The worst play of the day was the lack of urgency from both Rasha and Hassan around the wool metropolis. Hassan practically had it in his hands if he had played it right. Rasha seemed determined to hand Dania the metropolis for the win instead of taking it herself by trading her wool. In war, sometimes the smartest tactic is simple defense, and they could not execute it or prolong the game. They let Dania take the wool metropolis and seal the victory.

Lena sat out again, maybe scared off by the war-themed evening. Rola declared herself anti-violence and decided to stay home.

weeks.recapTitle: Abe's Trifecta: Best Play, Worst Play and the Win
weeks.bestPlay: Abe getting three points on his final turn to steal the win by breaking Hussein's longest road. It is hard to win when you have the worst play and the best play in the same week, but he is an enimga.
weeks.worstPlay: Abe used his spy to steal an irrigation card and gleefully played it without realizing the bank had no wheat left.
weeks.summary:
Abe finally got on the board with a midnight heist--snatching Longest Road and dropping three points in a single turn. A rare burst of decisiveness from the guy who usually thinks for five minutes and then accomplishes nothing.

Ali stuck to his usual strategy: tell everyone he has no chance of winning, then somehow end up right there again--until a dry spell and a badly timed 7 cost him the win.

Rasha showed up after months of just rolling dice and, in the second most surprising thing of the night, nearly won. We're counting that as a win for her.

Hassan had flashes of brilliance but, as usual, couldn't close. Second-worst play of the night: helping Ali save his city while Hussein and Rasha were about to explode.

And instead of Rasha rolling dice all night, Hussein took over as the designated roller--trash-talking loudly while extending his streak: another week without a win.

Lena stayed home, shocked that Abe went to game night while she was sick instead of taking care of her. Dania spent the night changing diapers while plotting how to make it next week.

We're still waiting on Rola to make her first appearance.
